lead: Air moves because a pressure difference pushes it. A pneumotachometer measures that push as a small drop across a known resistance, so the drop becomes flow, and flow integrated over time becomes volume. The pressures that drive the lung, inside the air sacs and in the space around the lung, cannot be reached with a probe, so they are found indirectly: from mouth pressure when the airway is briefly shut, and from a balloon in the oesophagus. These measurements appear in pulmonary function labs, ventilators and exercise testing, where a doctor needs to separate a blocked airway from a stiff lung.
prereq: You need: 2.5 for lung volumes, and the differential pressure transducer and carrier amplifier (see Physiological transducers and load cells).

blocks.text: The pneumotachometer is a deliberate resistance in the breathing path. Air crosses a fine mesh or a bundle of small tubes, and pressure taps before and after it feed a differential pressure transducer. For smooth, laminar flow the drop follows Poiseuille's law: it is proportional to flow. One calibration number, the resistance of the head, then links pressure drop and flow.

blocks.where: ΔP is the pressure drop in cm H₂O; R<sub>pt</sub> is the resistance of the pneumotachograph head in cm H₂O per L/s, its calibration factor; Q is the flow in L/s.

blocks.text: A Fleisch pneumotachograph uses many parallel capillaries: the parallel paths keep the total resistance low and the flow in each tube laminar. A screen pneumotachograph uses a woven wire mesh; it is cheaper but clogs with moisture more easily, so the head is often heated. A hot-wire flowmeter heats a thin wire and measures how much the flow cools it; it has no mesh and no simple pressure-drop law.

items: Set zero with no flow through the head.
Apply known steady flows across the working range. If 0.5 L/s gives 0.75 cm H₂O, R<sub>pt</sub> = 0.75/0.5 = 1.5 cm H₂O per L/s; equal ratios at 0.5, 1 and 2 L/s show the head is linear.
Keep flow inside the laminar range; turbulence makes the drop rise faster than flow.
Integrate the flow signal to get volume, and check the volume with a 3 L syringe pushed at slow and fast speeds.

sections.h3: Pressures inside and around the alveoli

blocks.text: Intra-alveolar pressure (Palv) is the pressure inside the air sacs. No sensor can sit in an air sac, so it is found indirectly. In the interrupter method a fast shutter closes the mouthpiece for about 0.1 s; flow stops, pressure equalises along the airway, and the mouth pressure just after closure equals the alveolar pressure just before it. The body plethysmograph gives it from the box pressure (see 2.8).

Intrapleural pressure (Ppl) is the pressure in the thin space between lung and chest wall. It is estimated with a thin balloon catheter in the lower oesophagus, because oesophageal pressure follows pleural pressure. Three differences are used: transpulmonary pressure, across the lung, Palv − Ppl; chest-wall (transthoracic) pressure, Ppl − Pbs, where Pbs is body-surface (atmospheric) pressure; and transrespiratory pressure, Palv − Pbs, across the whole system. Pressures are in cm H₂O; 1 cm H₂O = 0.098 kPa. At rest, intrapleural pressure is about −5 cm H₂O and alveolar pressure swings about ±1 cm H₂O.

blocks.where: P<sub>tp</sub> is transpulmonary pressure, P<sub>alv</sub> intra-alveolar pressure and P<sub>pl</sub> intrapleural pressure, all in cm H₂O and all measured from the same reference.

blocks.text: Airway resistance (Raw) links flow and the pressure that drives it. With expiratory flow taken as positive, Palv = Pmouth + Raw × Q; during inspiration alveolar pressure falls below mouth pressure. So Raw = (Palv − Pmouth) / Q, with Q read by the pneumotachometer just before the interruption. A narrowed airway raises Raw and needs a larger pressure difference for the same flow.

The differential transducer measures only the small drop across the head, often under 2 cm H₂O, so it needs good sensitivity and a stable zero. A carrier amplifier excites the transducer and demodulates its output into a voltage proportional to ΔP. The flow signal is then integrated to give volume.

blocks.where: V is volume in L; Q is flow in L/s; t is time in s.

blocks.text: Integration accumulates any offset: a zero error of 0.01 L/s for 60 s adds 0.6 L of false volume. Modern instruments reset the integrator at the start of each breath or subtract a measured zero. The same flow signal drives the volume display and the flow-volume loop. A clogged or wet mesh raises R<sub>pt</sub>, so the head is recalibrated with known flows, and the volume with a syringe, before each session.

figure.caption: Flow through the capillary bundle drops the pressure from P₁ to P₂. In the worked example 0.5 L/s gives 0.75 cm H₂O, so R<sub>pt</sub> = 1.5 cm H₂O per L/s; integrating 0.5 L/s for 1 s gives 0.5 L.

spec.aria: A pneumotachograph tube with a capillary bundle, pressure taps P1 and P2 feeding a differential transducer, then amplifier, flow and integrator blocks; 0.75 cm water at 0.5 litres per second, volume 0.5 litre.

examples.question: A Fleisch pneumotachograph gives a differential pressure of 0.75 cm H₂O at a steady flow of 0.5 L/s. (a) Find its resistance R<sub>pt</sub>. (b) During a 1 s inspiration the drop averages 0.75 cm H₂O; find the volume inspired. (c) A subject breathes out steadily through it; the reading is 0.75 cm H₂O when an interrupter shutter closes, and mouth pressure then rises to 1.0 cm H₂O. Find the flow and the airway resistance. (d) An oesophageal balloon reads −5 cm H₂O at that moment; find the transpulmonary pressure.
steps: (a) R<sub>pt</sub> = ΔP/Q = 0.75 cm H₂O ÷ 0.5 L/s = 1.5 cm H₂O per L/s.
(b) Average flow = 0.75/1.5 = 0.5 L/s; volume = 0.5 L/s × 1 s = 0.5 L.

(c) Flow before closure Q = 0.75/1.5 = 0.5 L/s. Mouth pressure after closure equals alveolar pressure before it: P<sub>alv</sub> = 1.0 cm H₂O, while mouth pressure during flow was 0. R<sub>aw</sub> = (1.0 − 0)/0.5 = 2.0 cm H₂O per L/s.
examples.answer: R<sub>pt</sub> = 1.5 cm H₂O per L/s; tidal volume 0.5 L; flow 0.5 L/s and R<sub>aw</sub> = 2.0 cm H₂O per L/s; transpulmonary pressure 6.0 cm H₂O.

traps: Mixing pressure references: airway and pneumotachometer pressures are gauge pressures, measured from atmosphere. A difference such as transpulmonary pressure is the same in any reference, but subtracting a gauge value from an absolute one gives nonsense.
Sign convention: with expiratory flow positive, P<sub>alv</sub> = P<sub>mouth</sub> + R<sub>aw</sub> × Q; inspiratory flow reverses the sign. A sign slip turns −1 cm H₂O into +1 cm H₂O.
Linear only while laminar: R<sub>pt</sub> is invalid once flow becomes turbulent, so high-flow readings need a linearisation curve or a larger head.
Unit slip: 1 cm H₂O is about 0.098 kPa, not 1 kPa, and about 0.74 mmHg, not 1 mmHg.
Intra-alveolar is not intrapleural: alveolar pressure is inside the air sac and swings around zero; intrapleural pressure is around the lung and stays below atmospheric in quiet breathing.

quiz.q: State the relation between pressure drop and flow in a linear pneumotachometer.
quiz.a: ΔP = R × Q, where ΔP is in cm H2O, R is in cm H2O per L/s and Q is in L/s. It holds while flow is laminar.

quiz.q: Why does a Fleisch pneumotachograph use many capillaries instead of one narrow tube?
quiz.a: Many parallel tubes give the needed laminar resistance with a low pressure drop, so the patient breathes without much extra work.

quiz.q: A pneumotachometer gives 0.90 cm H₂O at 0.60 L/s. Find its resistance R<sub>pt</sub>.
Explain why turbulence makes the pneumotachometer read wrongly at high flow.
quiz.a: Turbulent pressure drop rises roughly with Q², not Q, so the fixed linear calibration misreads high flows.

quiz.q: Airway resistance is 3 cm H2O per L/s, expiratory flow is 0.4 L/s and mouth pressure is 0. Find alveolar pressure. If intrapleural pressure is −6 cm H2O, find transpulmonary pressure.
quiz.a: P<sub>alv</sub> = 0 + 3 × 0.4 = 1.2 cm H₂O; P<sub>tp</sub> = 1.2 − (−6) = 7.2 cm H₂O.

quiz.q: How is intrapleural pressure estimated without a needle in the pleural space?
quiz.a: An oesophageal balloon measures oesophageal pressure, which closely follows pleural pressure.

quiz.q: A flow integrator has a zero offset of 0.02 L/s. What volume error appears after 30 s? What happens if the offset is not corrected?
quiz.a: Error = 0.02 × 30 = 0.6 L. Uncorrected, it adds a steady false ramp, so the volume trace climbs off the page and every volume read from it is wrong.

beyond: Not for the exam. Modern pneumotachometers often use a hot-wire or a differential-pressure sensor with digital linearisation, and some sleep-lab devices use a Pitot-tube mask. Research ventilators use fast pressure sensors and model-based estimates of alveolar pressure instead of a shutter. Search for respiratory mechanics, oesophageal balloon catheters, and flow integration drift if you want the instrumentation detail.
